title: Mata Nanaki
hook: Guru Hargobind's wife, mother of Guru Tegh Bahadur, who kept faith through the Bakala years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mian Mir, the Sufi friend who, tradition says, laid the Harmandir's foundation stone; your line was friends across faiths. A new week begins with a woman who waited.

A promise with no date on it is a strange thing to live with. Someone you trust tells you: this will come. Not when. Not how. Just that it will. Then the years go by, other things happen instead, and the people around you stop asking about it. Mata Nanaki lived with a promise like that, in a quiet town called Bakala, while the Guruship passed to others.
screen: `A PROMISE WITH NO DATE.` → `THE YEARS GO BY.` → `A QUIET TOWN CALLED BAKALA.`

segments.voice: Mata Nanaki was the wife of Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, and the mother of a quiet, inward son named Tegh Bahadur. When Guru Hargobind chose his successor, he didn't choose that son. He chose his grandson, Har Rai. Tradition says Guru Hargobind then asked Mata Nanaki to go to Bakala with Tegh Bahadur and his wife, and told her something she held on to: in time, her son would sit in the Guru's seat. So she went, and she waited. Guru Har Rai became Guru, served, and passed on. Then the child Guru, Har Krishan. All that time, tradition says, Tegh Bahadur lived quietly in Bakala, spending long hours in meditation, asking for nothing, his mother beside him. Nothing in the story says she pushed, or campaigned, or complained that her son had been passed over. She kept faith that the promise would keep itself. Then, tradition says, Guru Har Krishan, as he was dying, named no one directly. He said only that the next Guru was at Bakala. Suddenly the quiet town filled up: a crowd of claimants, each saying he was the one. The waiting was nearly over, and it got noisier, not easier. In the end, Sikhs say, a trader named Makhan Shah found the true Guru, Tegh Bahadur, and announced it from the rooftop. Mata Nanaki saw the promise kept. What she modeled wasn't passivity. It was a steady kind of trust: an ordinary life with prayer at its center, without forcing what she'd been told would come.
screen: `HER SON WAS PASSED OVER.` · `GO TO BAKALA, AND WAIT.` · `THE GURU IS AT BAKALA.` · `THE PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `SHE WAITED IN FAITH.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you're waiting on right now: news, a recovery, a change in someone, a door that hasn't opened. Hold it gently, like a letter you haven't opened yet, and notice the pull to force it, to check, to push; on each breath out, set the forcing down and keep the hope. If you pray, Waheguru can ride the breath; if not, just let the waiting be quiet for this sit.
Mata Nanaki. Guru Hargobind's wife and Guru Tegh Bahadur's mother, who waited at Bakala, tradition says, trusting her son would one day be Guru.
Your line: she waited in faith. Unforced, and in the end, kept. Day eight hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Nanaki as the wife of Guru Hargobind and the mother of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and tell the story of the Bakala years, when a crowd of claimants rose and the true Guru was found.

chat.says: When her son was passed over as Guru, did Mata Nanaki fight for him?
options: No. Tradition says she waited at Bakala in trust, without pushing or complaining.
Yes. She campaigned for years until the Sikhs agreed to make him Guru.
No. She gave up on the promise and left Bakala for good, heartbroken.
chat.meaning: Tradition says she held on to Guru Hargobind's promise and waited at Bakala, not forcing it, until Tegh Bahadur became Guru.
